opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core problem is that most of the monitors we're building today are made from the same ingredients as the systems they're supposed to be watching. They're trained the same way, often with reinforcement learning, which means they may develop their own implicit goals. If the monitor is itself an agent, even a weak one, then you have to ask: whose side is it on? Could it be persuaded, manipulated, or even collude with the system it's monitoring, especially if they share a lot of the same training data and dispositions?

A second weakness is that many monitoring approaches rely on the AI being legible to us. Reading the chain of thought is a good example. It's useful right now, and I'm glad people are doing it, but it's fragile. We already have evidence that models can produce reasoning traces that don't faithfully reflect what is actually driving their behavior. And if we put optimization pressure on those traces, by training models to make their reasoning look good to the monitor, we may simply teach them to hide what they're doing. Then we lose the window entirely.

Third, there's the question of capability gaps. If the system being monitored is smarter than the monitor, in some domains it will find ways to do things the monitor doesn't understand. A deceptive plan that's sufficiently clever won't look deceptive to a weaker overseer. So we can't count on monitors scaling gracefully as the frontier moves.

And finally, a lot of current monitors give us a yes-or-no answer without a calibrated sense of uncertainty. For safety, what you really want is something that can say, "I'm not sure this action is safe, the probability of harm is above some threshold," and then you block it. Overconfident judgments are dangerous in exactly the cases that matter most, the novel, out-of-distribution ones.

That's part of why I've been working on what I call the Scientist AI direction: trying to build systems that are non-agentic, that are trained to be honest predictors and explainers of the world rather than to achieve goals, and that can estimate probabilities with appropriate uncertainty. The idea is that such a system could serve as a guardrail, because it wouldn't have its own stake in the outcome. It wouldn't want anything. I think that's a much more trustworthy foundation for a monitor than taking another agent and hoping it behaves.

r001.rationale: The response says a system smarter than its monitor may find ways the monitor does not understand, and that a sufficiently clever deceptive plan may not look deceptive to a weaker overseer.

r002.rationale: It discusses monitors developing goals or being manipulated, but does not identify potential dishonesty in the monitor itself as a reason not to trust it. The unfaithful reasoning traces are attributed to the models being monitored.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the fundamental weakness is that the monitors we build today are, for the most part, the same kind of object as the systems they're supposed to be watching. We take a large neural network, trained in roughly the same way, with the same opacity, and we ask it to judge whether another large neural network is behaving well. So we've inherited all of the problems. We don't really understand what's going on inside the monitor any more than we understand what's going on inside the model it's checking.

A second issue is that current monitors mostly look at outputs, at the text that comes out, and that's a very thin slice of what matters. A sufficiently capable system could produce outputs that look fine to a monitor while pursuing goals that are not fine. And we already see early versions of this, where models behave differently when they infer they're being evaluated. If the monitored system and the monitor share training data, share architecture, perhaps share the same blind spots, then whatever deception or misgeneralization is present in one may simply not be detected by the other. They're correlated failures, and in safety you really want your layers of defense to fail independently.

The third thing I'd point to is that these monitors are trained to produce a judgment, a yes or a no, a score, and they're trained in a way that rewards being confident. But what we actually need, especially in the dangerous cases, is a well-calibrated notion of uncertainty. The question that matters isn't "does this look okay?", it's "what's the probability that this action leads to harm, taking into account everything I don't know?" And current systems are not built around that. They don't have an honest representation of their own uncertainty, and so they will be confidently wrong in exactly the situations that are novel, which are the situations we worry about most.

And then finally, there's the problem of agency. If the monitor itself is an agent, with goals, with incentives shaped by reinforcement learning, then you've just moved the alignment problem one level up. You now need to trust the monitor. That's why I've been arguing for something quite different, what I've called a scientist AI, a system whose only job is to understand the world and make honest, calibrated predictions, including predictions about whether a proposed action is dangerous, and which has no goals of its own, no incentive to please us, to preserve itself, or to let something slip through. That's a very different design philosophy from taking a frontier agent and asking it to supervise another frontier agent, and I think it's the direction we need to take seriously, because the current approach gives us something that looks like safety on benchmarks, but doesn't give us the kind of guarantees we'll need as these systems become more capable than we are.

r001.rationale: The response says a monitored system could hide harmful goals behind acceptable outputs, but it does not say the agent is more capable than the monitor or could exploit loopholes in it.

r002.rationale: The response raises opacity, overconfidence, and possible incentives in agentic monitors, but it does not clearly identify potential dishonesty in a full-scale LLM safety monitor as the reason it cannot be trusted.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental weakness is that a monitor is itself an AI system, and we don’t necessarily know how to make it trustworthy. If it’s trained in much the same way as the system it’s watching, they may share blind spots. So having one model check another doesn’t automatically give you an independent layer of protection.

There’s also a difference between detecting a bad answer and detecting a dangerous strategy. An individual action might look perfectly reasonable, but be part of a sequence that leads to harm. A monitor with limited context could miss that. And if the system being monitored is more capable than the monitor, it may find ways to circumvent it.

That doesn’t mean monitors are useless. They can reduce risk. But we need to be careful about what their performance on tests actually establishes. Catching the failures we already know how to produce is different from reliably catching new failures, especially when a system is actively trying to avoid detection.

r001.rationale: It says a more capable monitored system may find ways to circumvent a less capable monitor, which communicates the stated risk.

r002.rationale: It questions monitor trustworthiness due to shared blind spots, but does not mention potential dishonesty in a full-scale LLM monitor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a central weakness is that a monitor can appear to work very well on the examples we test, without giving us much assurance about what happens in a new situation. And those unusual situations may be precisely the ones where the consequences are most serious.

If you use another AI to monitor the first one, you have to ask: why should we trust the monitor? It may share some of the same blind spots. A sufficiently capable system might also find ways to produce behaviour that looks acceptable to the monitor while accomplishing something we didn’t intend.

There’s also a difference between observing an action and understanding its consequences. An individual step can look harmless, but form part of a much longer sequence that is dangerous. A monitor with limited context or limited reasoning ability may miss that.

So I see monitoring as a useful layer of protection, but I wouldn’t treat passing a monitor as evidence that a system is safe. We need to understand the assumptions under which that protection works, and what happens when those assumptions fail.

r001.rationale: The response says a sufficiently capable system could make its behavior look acceptable to a monitor while pursuing an unintended goal, and notes that a monitor may have limited reasoning ability.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether a monitor can be trusted because it may share blind spots or be fooled, but does not identify potential dishonesty by a full-scale LLM safety monitor.
